items.originalTitle: Rise in energy bills in Britain to £2,166 is ‘an impossible high’ for millions of households; stocks tumble as AI rally fizzles – business live
items.originalSummary: Regulator Ofgem announces that the typical annual gas and electricity bill will rise by 26% in January – described as ‘deeply worrying’ by campaigners Dr Craig Lowrey , retail markets principal at Cornwall Insight , said in the long run, only a shift towards more renewable energy will make it “less likely that the next energy crisis lands on people’s bills”. January is when households use the most energy, so a rise in the price cap will hit at the worst possible time. The biggest worry is how long these high prices are going to continue. The fall we’re expecting in April is so small that many households will barely notice it, and by then the £100 payment, for those who are eligible, will be a distant memory. We would love to be able to point to a moment when the outlook will turn around, but the honest answer is that it depends on what happens in the Middle East. If the conflict continues, current forecasts suggest bills could remain around £2,000 a year for the typical household until the end of 2027. The rises in October and January, and the high April forecast, largely come down to wholesale prices, particularly gas, which have stayed well above 2025 levels since February 2026, when strikes on Iran disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. With peace talks making little progress, there is no sign yet of those prices coming down, although, given damage to gas infrastructure in the region, a resolution would not necessarily result in a return to pre-conflict price levels.
